questions.stem: A community health clinic is planning a sexual health outreach program. A physician on the planning committee is asked to estimate how much of overall population health outcomes is attributable to clinical health care itself, as opposed to social determinants of health. Which of the following is the best estimate?

explanation.summary: Health care accounts for only about 10-20% of overall health outcomes; social determinants account for the remaining 80-90%.
explanation.whyCorrect: Social determinants of health are the conditions and systems that shape people's opportunities to achieve health. Estimates attribute only 10-20% of overall health outcomes to health care, with social determinants making up the other 80-90%. This is why addressing barriers outside the exam room is central to improving sexual and reproductive health.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Clinical care contributes more than this; it is estimated at 10-20% of overall health outcomes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This underestimates the contribution of clinical care, which is estimated at 10-20%.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This overestimates the contribution of clinical care; social determinants account for the other 80-90%.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Clinical care is not the majority contributor; social determinants account for roughly 80-90% of health outcomes.

questions.topicName: Social Determinants of Sexual and Reproductive Health

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman comes for a postpartum visit 8 weeks after delivery. She has taken daily oral HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) throughout pregnancy and wants to continue it. Her pregnancy-related insurance coverage will end next month, and she works an hourly job without paid leave. She remains HIV negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to maintain her HIV prevention?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Advise her to take unpaid leave to attend more frequent office visits

choices.label: B
choices.text: Discontinue PrEP now and restart it once new insurance is secured

choices.label: C
choices.text: Document the coverage lapse and reassess PrEP at her annual visit

choices.label: D
choices.text: Refer for insurance navigation and a medication assistance program

choices.label: E
choices.text: Switch her to condoms alone because PrEP access is now uncertain

explanation.summary: When coverage eligibility changes, continuity of prevention depends on insurance navigation, medication assistance programs and other mechanisms that prevent gaps in medication access.
explanation.whyCorrect: Clinical appropriateness does not guarantee access: changes in insurance after pregnancy can interrupt preventive services such as PrEP. To create continuity of prevention, clinicians and health systems can use insurance navigation, medication assistance programs, pharmacy support, referral networks, telehealth, and coordination across services. Connecting her to navigation and assistance programs directly targets the barrier while preserving her chosen prevention strategy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Missing hourly shifts is itself a barrier to care; adding visits and lost income worsens access rather than solving it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Stopping PrEP creates exactly the gap in prevention that clinicians should work to prevent when eligibility for coverage changes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Deferring the problem leaves her without medication; continuity requires proactive navigation and mechanisms to prevent gaps.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The patient wants to continue PrEP; uncertain coverage is a barrier to address, not a reason to abandon her chosen prevention strategy.

questions.topicName: Social Determinants of Sexual and Reproductive Health

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman has experienced years of housing instability, food insecurity and workplace discrimination. She now has elevated inflammatory markers, insulin resistance and hypertension. Which of the following mechanisms best explains how her social circumstances became biologically embedded?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoimmune adrenal destruction with prolonged aldosterone loss

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chronic HPA axis suppression with prolonged cortisol deficiency

choices.label: C
choices.text: Exogenous glucocorticoid use with iatrogenic Cushing syndrome

choices.label: D
choices.text: Persistent HPA axis activation with prolonged cortisol exposure

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sustained parasympathetic dominance with low catecholamine output

explanation.summary: Adverse social determinants become biologically embedded through persistent HPA axis activation and prolonged cortisol exposure, producing allostatic load.
explanation.whyCorrect: Poverty, housing instability, food insecurity, discrimination and chronic stress persistently activate the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, prolonging cortisol exposure. Over time this produces allostatic load, which is associated with endocrine, cardiovascular, immune and metabolic dysregulation, increased inflammation and epigenetic changes that raise the risk of chronic disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autoimmune adrenal destruction is a primary adrenal disease, not the pathway through which chronic social stress is embedded.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Adverse social determinants cause persistent activation of the HPA axis, not suppression, with prolonged cortisol exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nothing in the history suggests medication exposure; the cortisol exposure in allostatic load is endogenous and stress-driven.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Chronic stress is not characterized by parasympathetic dominance; the lecture describes HPA axis activation and cortisol excess.

questions.topicName: Social Determinants of Sexual and Reproductive Health

questions.stem: A sexual health clinic finds that patients seeking abortion counseling and STI testing often leave before being seen. The medical director wants to address stigma at the structural level rather than the interpersonal level. Which of the following interventions best fits this goal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Asking clinicians to reassure each patient privately that they are not judged

choices.label: B
choices.text: Auditing confidentiality procedures, scheduling systems and referral pathways

choices.label: C
choices.text: Coaching clinicians to use neutral language when taking a sexual history

choices.label: D
choices.text: Encouraging each physician to introduce themselves warmly at every encounter

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reminding staff to avoid assumptions about the gender of a patient's partners

explanation.summary: Structural-level stigma reduction examines clinic policies, documentation, confidentiality procedures, scheduling systems and referral pathways; interpersonal-level work uses respectful, neutral language and avoids assumptions.
explanation.whyCorrect: Health professionals address stigma at two levels. At the interpersonal level, they use respectful, neutral language and avoid assumptions. At the structural level, they examine whether clinic policies, documentation, confidentiality procedures, scheduling systems and referral pathways make care realistically accessible. Auditing those systems is the structural intervention.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Individual reassurance is an interpersonal act; the structural level examines policies, documentation and pathways.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neutral, respectful language is an interpersonal-level strategy used within the individual clinician-patient encounter.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A warm introduction is an individual behavior within one encounter; it does not examine clinic policies or systems.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Avoiding assumptions is part of the interpersonal level of responsibility, not a structural change to clinic systems.

questions.topicName: Social Determinants of Sexual and Reproductive Health

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man in a town of 900 people has been prescribed HIV PrEP by a telehealth clinician. His insurance covers the medication, he owns a reliable car, and the only local pharmacy stocks it. He has not filled the prescription because the pharmacist is a close friend of his parents. Which of the following rural barriers best explains why he has not started PrEP?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absence of affordable insurance coverage for PrEP

choices.label: B
choices.text: Concern about confidentiality in a small community

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lack of a nearby pharmacy that stocks the medication

choices.label: D
choices.text: Limited public transportation to reach a pharmacy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Scarcity of clinicians who prescribe the medication

explanation.summary: In rural settings, concerns about confidentiality in small communities can block care even when prescribers, pharmacies, transportation and coverage are all available.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rural patients may face fewer prescribers, longer travel, limited public transportation, fewer pharmacies, limited specialty care and laboratory access, fewer after-hours appointments, and concerns about confidentiality in small communities. Every other barrier has been removed in this stem; his fear that a family friend will learn he is taking PrEP is a confidentiality barrier, and rurality often interacts with stigma in this way.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The stem states that his insurance covers the medication.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The local pharmacy stocks PrEP; the barrier is who he would encounter there, not supply.
whyWrongByChoice.D: He owns a reliable car, so transportation is not the barrier in this case.
whyWrongByChoice.E: He already has a prescription from a telehealth clinician, so prescriber availability is not limiting him.

questions.topicName: Social Determinants of Sexual and Reproductive Health

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman asks about her risk of acquiring HIV from her male partner. He has taken antiretroviral therapy for 6 years, and his records confirm a sustained undetectable HIV viral load. Neither partner has other potential HIV exposures. Which of the following statements is most accurate for her counseling?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He can still transmit HIV sexually unless condoms are used with every act

choices.label: B
choices.text: He does not sexually transmit HIV while his viral load stays undetectable

choices.label: C
choices.text: His risk of sexually transmitting HIV is lowered by about half on therapy

choices.label: D
choices.text: His undetectable status protects against vertical but not sexual transmission

choices.label: E
choices.text: His viral load must be undetectable for 10 years before transmission stops

explanation.summary: U = U: individuals who maintain an undetectable viral load on effective ART do not sexually transmit HIV.
explanation.whyCorrect: Effective antiretroviral therapy can suppress HIV viral load to undetectable levels, and individuals who maintain an undetectable viral load do not sexually transmit HIV to their partners. This principle, Undetectable = Untransmittable, is an important part of prevention counseling once sustained suppression is confirmed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: U = U means an undetectable viral load does not transmit sexually; condoms are not required to prevent HIV transmission in this setting.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sustained viral suppression does far more than halve risk; people who maintain an undetectable viral load do not sexually transmit HIV.
whyWrongByChoice.D: U = U specifically addresses sexual transmission: undetectable equals untransmittable.
whyWrongByChoice.E: No such duration is required; sustained suppression on effective therapy is the requirement.

questions.topicName: Social Determinants of Sexual and Reproductive Health

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man who has sex with men was treated for gonorrhea 3 months ago and for syphilis last year. He asks about doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis (doxy-PEP) and it is prescribed. Which of the following is the correct way for him to take it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 100 mg daily continuously for as long as he remains sexually active

choices.label: B
choices.text: 100 mg twice daily for 7 days beginning after each sexual exposure

choices.label: C
choices.text: A single 100 mg dose taken within 24 hours before anticipated sex

choices.label: D
choices.text: A single 200 mg dose as soon as possible, within 72 hours after sex

choices.label: E
choices.text: A single 200 mg dose taken at any time up to 7 days after sex

explanation.summary: Doxy-PEP is one 200 mg dose of doxycycline taken as soon as possible and no later than 72 hours after sexual exposure.
explanation.whyCorrect: The CDC recommends doxy-PEP for certain populations, including gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men and transgender women with a recent history of syphilis, chlamydia or gonorrhea. When prescribed, a single 200 mg dose is taken as soon as possible and no later than 72 hours after sexual exposure. This patient's recent gonorrhea and syphilis make him a candidate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Doxy-PEP is not a continuous daily regimen; it is a single dose after an exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This resembles a treatment course, not doxy-PEP, which is a single 200 mg dose after exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Doxy-PEP is taken after, not before, sexual exposure, and the dose is 200 mg.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The dose should be taken as soon as possible and no later than 72 hours after exposure, not up to 7 days.

questions.topicName: Social Determinants of Sexual and Reproductive Health

questions.stem: A 26-year-old breastfeeding woman wants HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis but has trouble with daily pills, keeping medications private at home and reaching a pharmacy each month. Her clinician describes an option given as a subcutaneous injection every six months. Which of the following medications is being described?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cabotegravir

choices.label: B
choices.text: Doxycycline

choices.label: C
choices.text: Emtricitabine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lenacapavir

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate

explanation.summary: Lenacapavir is long-acting HIV PrEP given by subcutaneous injection every six months.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lenacapavir provides HIV PrEP through a subcutaneous injection administered every six months and can be considered during breastfeeding. Its long dosing interval is attractive for patients facing barriers with daily adherence, privacy, medication storage, frequent pharmacy visits, transportation or unstable insurance coverage.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cabotegravir is another long-acting injectable PrEP option, but the twice-yearly subcutaneous agent is lenacapavir.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Doxycycline is used as post-exposure prophylaxis for bacterial STIs, not as HIV PrEP.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Emtricitabine is an oral component of daily oral PrEP, not a twice-yearly injection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate is taken orally every day as part of daily oral PrEP.

questions.topicName: Social Determinants of Sexual and Reproductive Health

questions.stem: At a quality meeting, data show higher rates of preterm delivery among Black patients in the health system than among White patients. A resident proposes that the difference reflects a single inherited biologic risk carried by Black patients. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ask what social and structural conditions produced the difference

choices.label: B
choices.text: Attribute the difference mainly to individual patient health choices

choices.label: C
choices.text: Conclude that the gap is explained entirely by differences in insurance

choices.label: D
choices.text: Set the data aside because racial categories are too imprecise to use

choices.label: E
choices.text: Treat race itself as the primary biologic risk factor for preterm birth

explanation.summary: When racial disparities are observed, avoid single-factor explanations and ask what social and structural conditions produced the difference.
explanation.whyCorrect: Structural racism can influence neighborhood resources, economic opportunity, insurance coverage, transportation, the availability and quality of care, exposure to discrimination, trust in health institutions and access to preventive services. Because multiple influences contribute to observed patterns, clinicians should be cautious about attributing disparities to any single factor and should ask what social and structural conditions produced the difference.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Attributing the gap to individual behavior is still a single-factor explanation and ignores structural influences on access and outcomes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Insurance is one of many influences of structural racism; attributing the gap to it alone repeats the single-factor error.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Disparities should be examined, not dismissed; the right step is to ask what conditions produced them.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The lecture cautions against attributing racial disparities to any single factor; structural conditions shape these outcomes.

questions.topicName: Social Determinants of Sexual and Reproductive Health

questions.stem: A medical student preparing to counsel adolescents is asked how the World Health Organization defines sexual health. Which of the following best reflects that definition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Consistent use of barrier contraception during all sexual activity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Normal sexual function confirmed by physical and laboratory examination

choices.label: C
choices.text: The ability to reproduce without complications of pregnancy or birth

choices.label: D
choices.text: The absence of sexually transmitted infections and sexual dysfunction

choices.label: E
choices.text: Well-being in relation to sexuality, not merely the absence of disease

explanation.summary: WHO defines sexual health as physical, emotional, mental and social well-being in relation to sexuality, not merely the absence of disease, dysfunction or infirmity.
explanation.whyCorrect: The World Health Organization describes sexual health as a state of physical, emotional, mental and social well-being in relation to sexuality; it is not merely the absence of disease, dysfunction or infirmity. It involves a respectful, evidence-based approach to sexuality and relationships, free from stigma, discrimination, coercion and violence.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A single behavior does not define sexual health, which is a state of physical, emotional, mental and social well-being.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The definition is not limited to physical function; it includes emotional, mental and social well-being.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sexual health is not defined by reproductive capacity; it concerns well-being in relation to sexuality.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The WHO definition explicitly states that sexual health is not merely the absence of disease, dysfunction or infirmity.

questions.topicName: Social Determinants of Sexual and Reproductive Health

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman seen for vaginal discharge discloses that she sometimes exchanges sex for a place to stay. She appears anxious and asks whether this will be written in her chart. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Advise her to stop exchanging sex for housing before any prevention options are offered

choices.label: B
choices.text: Assess her safety and possible coercion without assumptions, and offer HIV testing and PrEP

choices.label: C
choices.text: Notify law enforcement so that the exchange of sex for housing can be investigated

choices.label: D
choices.text: Postpone HIV prevention counseling until she has found stable housing of her own

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tell her that she lacks autonomy in these exchanges and refer her to a trafficking hotline

explanation.summary: For patients engaged in commercial or survival sex, provide confidential, trauma-informed care: assess safety and coercion without assumptions and offer testing and PrEP.
explanation.whyCorrect: Housing instability, violence, stigma, criminalization and difficulty negotiating protective measures can increase exposure to HIV and STIs, and confidentiality concerns can suppress care-seeking. Clinicians should provide respectful, confidential, trauma-informed care, assess safety and potential coercion without assumptions, and discuss HIV testing and PrEP options, including long-acting formulations, in a way that supports informed choice and autonomy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Care should be voluntary and patient-centered; requiring behavior change before offering prevention is a barrier to care.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reporting to police would undermine confidentiality and trust; criminalization is itself a structural factor that raises risk and deters care.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Delaying prevention leaves her exposed; testing and PrEP should be discussed now in a patient-centered way.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Clinicians should not assume a patient's circumstances or level of autonomy based solely on disclosure of commercial or survival sex.

questions.topicName: Social Determinants of Sexual and Reproductive Health

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman who is 3 months postpartum and exclusively breastfeeding wants to start HIV PrEP because her partner's HIV care was recently interrupted. She has stable insurance, a pharmacy next to her office and says she prefers taking a pill each morning with her vitamins. Her current HIV test is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate PrEP regimen for her?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Daily oral cabotegravir taken until breastfeeding ends

choices.label: B
choices.text: Daily oral emtricitabine monotherapy until weaning is complete

choices.label: C
choices.text: Daily oral tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Single 200 mg doxycycline dose after each sexual exposure

choices.label: E
choices.text: Subcutaneous lenacapavir injection given every 6 months

explanation.summary: Daily oral TDF/FTC has been widely studied in pregnancy and breastfeeding and suits a patient who prefers a daily oral strategy; the choice comes from shared decision-making.
explanation.whyCorrect: PrEP options discussed during breastfeeding include daily oral tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine, long-acting injectable lenacapavir and long-acting injectable cabotegravir. TDF/FTC has been widely studied in pregnant and breastfeeding populations and suits patients who prefer a daily oral strategy. Because this patient states that preference and has no adherence, storage, pharmacy or coverage barriers, shared decision-making points to daily oral TDF/FTC.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cabotegravir is discussed as a long-acting injectable PrEP option, not a daily oral regimen for this purpose.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Emtricitabine alone is not a PrEP regimen; the oral option studied in breastfeeding is tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Doxy-PEP prevents bacterial STIs, not HIV, and is not HIV PrEP.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lenacapavir is an option, but she prefers a daily pill and has none of the barriers its long interval is meant to overcome.

questions.topicName: Social Determinants of Sexual and Reproductive Health

questions.stem: A county health department is tracking adolescent pregnancy rates as a marker of sexual and reproductive health inequity. Which of the following age ranges defines adolescent pregnancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 10-19 years

choices.label: B
choices.text: 10-21 years

choices.label: C
choices.text: 12-17 years

choices.label: D
choices.text: 13-18 years

choices.label: E
choices.text: 15-21 years

explanation.summary: Adolescent pregnancy is pregnancy in an individual 10-19 years of age and carries increased maternal, neonatal and socioeconomic risks.
explanation.whyCorrect: Adolescent pregnancy is defined as pregnancy occurring between 10 and 19 years of age. Compared with pregnancy in adults, it is associated with increased maternal, neonatal and socioeconomic risks, and socioeconomic factors are associated with its rates.

whyWrongByChoice.B: This range extends into adulthood; adolescent pregnancy ends at 19 years of age.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This range is too narrow; adolescent pregnancy is defined as pregnancy between 10 and 19 years of age.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This range omits both younger adolescents and 19-year-olds; the definition is 10-19 years.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This range excludes younger adolescents and includes adults; the definition is 10-19 years.

questions.topicName: Social Determinants of Sexual and Reproductive Health

questions.stem: A public health lecturer illustrates how income shapes health using U.S. data on men. She compares the average life expectancy of men in the top 1% of the income distribution with that of men in the bottom 1%. Which of the following best approximates the difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 2 years

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 5 years

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 10 years

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 20 years

choices.label: E
choices.text: About 35 years

explanation.summary: U.S. men in the top 1% of income live over 82 years on average versus about 63 years in the bottom 1%, a gap of almost 20 years.
explanation.whyCorrect: A 2016 analysis found that U.S. men in the top 1% of income had a life expectancy longer than the average man in any other country (more than 82 years), while men in the bottom 1% had a life expectancy of about 63 years, comparable to countries with inadequate health infrastructure. The difference is almost 20 years, showing that income affects health well beyond the ability to pay a bill.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The gap is far larger: over 82 years in the top 1% versus about 63 years in the bottom 1%.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This understates the gap; top-1% men live more than 82 years versus about 63 in the bottom 1%.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This is roughly half the actual gap of almost 20 years.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This overstates the gap; the difference is almost 20 years (over 82 versus about 63).

questions.topicName: Social Determinants of Sexual and Reproductive Health

questions.stem: During sign-out, a resident describes a 33-year-old woman who missed her postpartum blood pressure check and her contraception visit as 'noncompliant.' The attending asks the team to reframe how they think about her missed care. Which of the following questions best reflects that reframing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: How can we document her nonadherence clearly in the medical record?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Should she be discharged from the practice after repeated no-shows?

choices.label: C
choices.text: What factors or barriers stood between her and the care she needed?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Which counseling approach will convince her that follow-up matters?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Why did she choose not to come in for the care we offered her?

explanation.summary: Instead of asking why a patient did not get care, ask what factors or barriers stood between the patient and the care they needed.
explanation.whyCorrect: The lecture explicitly recommends replacing 'Why didn't this patient get care?' with 'What factors or barriers stood between this patient and the care they needed?' This shifts attention to social determinants such as transportation, work schedules, childcare, insurance and cost that commonly explain missed visits.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Documenting nonadherence labels the patient rather than identifying the barriers that prevented her from getting care.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Discharging the patient punishes the result of barriers and further reduces her access to care.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This assumes the problem is her motivation rather than the structural and social barriers she faces.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This framing places responsibility on the patient's choices, which is the approach the lecture asks clinicians to move away from.

questions.topicName: Social Determinants of Sexual and Reproductive Health

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman with chronic hypertension has missed three appointments since delivery, and her blood pressure remains uncontrolled despite an appropriate medication regimen. She works two jobs with little paid time off, has no reliable car and often skips meals to feed her children. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Counsel her on the risks of uncontrolled hypertension to improve adherence

choices.label: B
choices.text: Document her missed visits and send a warning letter about dismissal policy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Engage a social worker for transportation and food resources

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increase her antihypertensive dose and schedule a return visit in 2 weeks

choices.label: E
choices.text: Refer her to a hypertension specialist at the academic center 90 miles away

explanation.summary: When social barriers undermine appropriate treatment, the team should partner with social work and community resources for transportation, nutrition and support.
explanation.whyCorrect: Poorly controlled chronic disease despite appropriate treatment, missed visits, unreliable transportation, multiple jobs with limited paid leave and food insecurity point to social determinants rather than a medical failure. The appropriate response is to collaborate with a social worker and community partners to provide transportation assistance, nutrition resources and community-based support programs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Education does not solve lack of transportation, limited paid time off or food insecurity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Punitive responses do not address the social determinants underlying her missed appointments.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Her regimen is already appropriate; the problem is access and social barriers, and another in-person visit repeats the barrier.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Specialty referral at a distance adds travel and missed work without addressing the barriers driving poor control.

questions.topicName: Social Determinants of Sexual and Reproductive Health

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman on HIV PrEP lives 75 miles from the nearest sexual health clinic, has no public transportation, and cannot leave work during clinic hours. She has missed two scheduled counseling follow-up visits but has kept her lab appointments at a nearby hospital lab. Which of the following changes would most directly support her continued prevention?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mailing her written materials about the importance of follow-up

choices.label: B
choices.text: Offering telehealth follow-up visits when clinically appropriate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pausing PrEP until she can attend visits during clinic hours

choices.label: D
choices.text: Requiring an in-person visit before each prescription refill

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transferring her care to a clinic in the nearest large city

explanation.summary: Telehealth, when appropriate, is one tool for maintaining continuity of prevention for patients facing distance and work-schedule barriers.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rural patients face longer travel distances, limited public transportation and fewer appointments outside working hours. Measures that create continuity of prevention include insurance navigation, medication assistance, pharmacy support, referral networks, telehealth when appropriate and coordination across services. Because her labs are already obtained locally, telehealth addresses the remaining barrier to counseling visits.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Her problem is distance and scheduling, not a lack of information about follow-up.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pausing prevention creates a gap in medication access rather than addressing the barrier.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Adding in-person requirements increases travel and lost work, the very barriers limiting her care.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A distant city clinic worsens travel distance and does not address her work-hours conflict.

questions.topicName: Social Determinants of Sexual and Reproductive Health

questions.stem: A 41-year-old Black woman declines a recommended preventive service after saying that her family has had repeated negative experiences with local hospitals over several generations. She has insurance and lives near the clinic. Which influence of structural racism is most directly reflected in her decision?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fewer neighborhood clinical resources

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lack of access to transportation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Limited insurance coverage

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reduced trust in health institutions

choices.label: E
choices.text: Restricted economic opportunity

explanation.summary: Structural racism can erode trust in health institutions, which can reduce use of preventive services even when coverage and proximity are adequate.
explanation.whyCorrect: Structural racism may influence neighborhood resources, economic opportunity, insurance coverage, transportation, availability and quality of care, exposure to discrimination, trust in health institutions and access to preventive services. With coverage and proximity in place, her decision rooted in generations of negative experiences reflects diminished trust in health institutions.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A clinic is nearby; the barrier is her family's experience with institutions, not resource scarcity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: She lives near the clinic, so transportation does not explain her decision.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The stem states that she has insurance, so coverage is not the limiting influence.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nothing in the stem points to income or employment as the reason she declined.

questions.topicName: Social Determinants of Sexual and Reproductive Health

questions.stem: A clinician is updating the intake form at a primary care practice. The form should distinguish sexual orientation from related concepts. Which of the following best defines sexual orientation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A person's internal sense of their own gender

choices.label: B
choices.text: Patterns of emotional, romantic, or sexual attraction

choices.label: C
choices.text: The number of sexual partners a person has had

choices.label: D
choices.text: The sex a person was assigned at birth

choices.label: E
choices.text: The specific sexual practices a person engages in

explanation.summary: Sexual orientation describes patterns of emotional, romantic or sexual attraction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sexual orientation is a characteristic that describes patterns of emotional, romantic or sexual attraction. It is distinct from gender identity, sex assigned at birth and specific sexual behaviors, each of which may be asked about separately in a comprehensive sexual history.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An internal sense of gender describes gender identity, not sexual orientation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Partner number is part of a sexual history, not a definition of orientation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sex assigned at birth is a separate characteristic from sexual orientation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sexual practices are behaviors; orientation describes patterns of attraction.

questions.topicName: Social Determinants of Sexual and Reproductive Health

questions.stem: A medical history seminar reviews the early HIV/AIDS epidemic in the United States, when gay and bisexual men carried a high burden of disease and HIV became closely linked with homosexuality in public discourse. Which of the following became an important force in advancing HIV research, treatment access, public education, and protection from discrimination?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Advocacy by affected communities

choices.label: B
choices.text: Criminal penalties for HIV exposure

choices.label: C
choices.text: Exclusion of affected groups from trials

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mandatory quarantine of affected groups

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced public attention to the epidemic

explanation.summary: Community advocacy was a major force advancing HIV research, access to treatment, public education and protection from discrimination.
explanation.whyCorrect: During the early HIV/AIDS epidemic, gay and bisexual men were among the populations with a high burden of disease, and HIV became closely associated with homosexuality in public discourse, shaping perceptions of both HIV and LGBTQ+ communities. Community advocacy became an important force in advancing HIV research, access to treatment, public education and protection from discrimination.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Criminalization is described as a barrier to care, not a force that advanced education or anti-discrimination protections.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Exclusion from research would impede, not advance, HIV research and treatment access.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Quarantine is not described as advancing research or protections; community advocacy drove those gains.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Less attention would slow progress; organized advocacy increased attention, research and access.

questions.topicName: Social Determinants of Sexual and Reproductive Health

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman mentions that her husband, who is living with HIV, had male partners before their marriage. She wants to understand her own current risk of acquiring HIV from him. Which of the following questions about her husband is most informative for assessing her risk?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Does he currently identify himself as gay or bisexual?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Has he told his family members about his orientation?

choices.label: C
choices.text: How long ago did he last have sex with another man?

choices.label: D
choices.text: How many male partners did he have before the marriage?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Is he taking ART with a sustained, suppressed viral load?

explanation.summary: A partner's history of sex with men is one part of the history; current HIV risk hinges on whether he is on ART with sustained viral suppression and whether other exposures exist.
explanation.whyCorrect: A partner's prior sexual relationships with men is one component of a comprehensive sexual history and should be considered alongside other factors. When evaluating HIV transmission risk, clinicians consider whether the partner is taking antiretroviral therapy, whether his viral load is suppressed, whether suppression is sustained, whether there are other exposures for either partner and what prevention strategy the patient wants.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Orientation is one component of a history and does not by itself determine whether he can transmit HIV now.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Disclosure to family is unrelated to his current ability to transmit HIV.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Timing of past male partners matters less than whether he is on ART with sustained suppression.
whyWrongByChoice.D: His past partner number does not determine current transmission risk; his treatment and viral suppression do.

questions.topicName: Social Determinants of Sexual and Reproductive Health

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman whose partner has had a sustained undetectable HIV viral load for 5 years understands that he does not sexually transmit HIV. She still asks to start PrEP because she wants an additional layer of protection. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Advise her that PrEP is reserved for partners with detectable virus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decline PrEP because U = U makes additional protection pointless

choices.label: C
choices.text: Discuss PrEP options that fit her goals and preferences

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prescribe PrEP only if her partner agrees to stop his own ART

choices.label: E
choices.text: Require 12 months of partner viral load reports before prescribing

explanation.summary: Even when U = U applies, a patient may choose PrEP; the discussion is guided by her goals, values and prevention needs.
explanation.whyCorrect: Understanding U = U is important in counseling, but a patient may nevertheless choose PrEP based on her circumstances, preferences or desire for an additional prevention strategy. Discussions about PrEP should be guided by the patient's goals, values and prevention needs rather than the clinician's assumptions.

whyWrongByChoice.A: PrEP is not restricted in this way; her preferences and prevention needs guide the decision.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Patients may still choose PrEP based on circumstances, preferences or desire for an additional strategy; PrEP discussion follows her goals.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Stopping his ART would end his viral suppression; there is no basis for tying her PrEP to his treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.E: No such requirement is described; her request should be addressed through shared decision-making.

questions.topicName: Social Determinants of Sexual and Reproductive Health

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman who is 6 weeks postpartum and breastfeeding reports ongoing sexual exposure to a partner living with HIV whose viral load status is unknown. She asks about HIV prevention. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step to guide counseling?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Current HIV testing and an individualized exposure assessment

choices.label: B
choices.text: Starting doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis after sex

choices.label: C
choices.text: Stopping breastfeeding before any prevention is discussed

choices.label: D
choices.text: Testing the infant for HIV before counseling the mother

choices.label: E
choices.text: Waiting until 6 months postpartum to begin any prevention

explanation.summary: For a breastfeeding patient with ongoing HIV exposure, current HIV testing and individualized exposure assessment guide prevention counseling.
explanation.whyCorrect: Postpartum and breastfeeding patients may benefit from HIV prevention discussions when ongoing exposure is present. Current HIV testing and an individualized assessment of exposure guide counseling and prevention options. Her partner can also be offered support in accessing HIV care and viral load monitoring, and if sustained suppression is confirmed, counseling may include U = U.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Doxy-PEP prevents bacterial STIs, not HIV, and is not the initial step in HIV prevention counseling.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Breastfeeding does not preclude prevention; several PrEP options can be discussed during breastfeeding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Counseling for the mother begins with her own current HIV testing and exposure assessment.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Postpartum breastfeeding patients with ongoing exposure may benefit from prevention discussions now, not after a delay.

questions.topicName: Social Determinants of Sexual and Reproductive Health

questions.stem: A 30-year-old pregnant woman is reviewing HIV PrEP choices. She is told that, in addition to lenacapavir, there is another long-acting injectable PrEP agent that may be considered during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Which of the following is this agent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cabotegravir

choices.label: B
choices.text: Doxycycline

choices.label: C
choices.text: Emtricitabine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tenofovir

choices.label: E
choices.text: Zidovudine

explanation.summary: Cabotegravir is a long-acting injectable PrEP option that may be considered during pregnancy and breastfeeding.
explanation.whyCorrect: PrEP approaches appropriate for discussion during breastfeeding include daily oral tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine, long-acting injectable lenacapavir and long-acting injectable cabotegravir. Cabotegravir is another injectable PrEP strategy that may be considered during pregnancy and breastfeeding.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Doxycycline is used as post-exposure prophylaxis for bacterial STIs, not as injectable HIV PrEP.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Emtricitabine is an oral agent used in daily oral PrEP with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate is part of the daily oral PrEP regimen, not a long-acting injectable.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Zidovudine is not among the PrEP options described; the other injectable PrEP option is cabotegravir.

questions.topicName: Social Determinants of Sexual and Reproductive Health

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman in a rural county switches from daily oral PrEP to lenacapavir injections every 6 months because she had trouble hiding pill bottles from relatives and refilling monthly at a pharmacy 40 miles away. Which of the following barriers is the new regimen least likely to eliminate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Need for adherence to a pill taken every day

choices.label: B
choices.text: Need for evaluation, lab testing and follow-up

choices.label: C
choices.text: Need for monthly trips to refill a prescription

choices.label: D
choices.text: Need to keep medication bottles private at home

choices.label: E
choices.text: Need to store a medication supply at home

explanation.summary: Long-acting PrEP eases daily adherence, privacy, storage and refill barriers, but effectiveness still depends on access to evaluation, lab testing, coverage, transportation and follow-up.
explanation.whyCorrect: A medication given twice yearly may reduce challenges associated with daily medication use or frequent refills. However, the effectiveness of any prevention strategy still depends on access to healthcare services, including clinical evaluation, laboratory testing, medication coverage, transportation and follow-up care. Those requirements persist with lenacapavir.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Twice-yearly injections remove the need for daily pill adherence.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A 6-month interval removes frequent pharmacy refills.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Injectable dosing avoids keeping pills at home, easing privacy concerns.
whyWrongByChoice.E: With clinic-administered injections there is no home supply to store.

questions.topicName: Social Determinants of Sexual and Reproductive Health

questions.stem: A sexual health clinic is implementing CDC guidance on doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis (doxy-PEP). Which of the following patients is the best candidate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A breastfeeding woman seeking protection from HIV

choices.label: B
choices.text: A heterosexual man requesting HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis

choices.label: C
choices.text: A man who has sex with men and has never had a bacterial STI

choices.label: D
choices.text: A transgender woman starting HIV PrEP with no STI history

choices.label: E
choices.text: A transgender woman treated for chlamydia 4 months ago

explanation.summary: CDC recommends doxy-PEP for groups including MSM and transgender women with a recent history of syphilis, chlamydia or gonorrhea.
explanation.whyCorrect: Doxy-PEP is a bacterial STI prevention strategy that the CDC recommends for certain populations, including gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men and transgender women with a recent history of syphilis, chlamydia or gonorrhea. A transgender woman recently treated for chlamydia fits this recommendation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Doxy-PEP prevents bacterial STIs, not HIV; HIV prevention is addressed with PrEP.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Doxy-PEP is not HIV PrEP, and he has no recent bacterial STI.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The recommendation targets MSM and transgender women with a recent history of syphilis, chlamydia or gonorrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Without a recent history of syphilis, chlamydia or gonorrhea, she is not in the recommended group.

questions.topicName: Social Determinants of Sexual and Reproductive Health

questions.stem: Researchers compare pregnancy outcomes between patients in the lowest and highest socioeconomic groups within the same region. Based on reported associations, which of the following findings is most expected in the lowest socioeconomic group?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Higher rates of obstetric hemorrhage

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lower rates of caesarean delivery

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lower rates of preeclampsia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lower rates of preterm delivery

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lower rates of unintended pregnancy

explanation.summary: Lower socioeconomic status is associated with more unintended and adolescent pregnancy, STIs, and complications such as caesarean delivery, preeclampsia, preterm delivery and obstetric hemorrhage.
explanation.whyCorrect: Studies have associated socioeconomic factors with rates of unintended pregnancy, adolescent pregnancy, sexually transmitted infections and certain pregnancy-related complications, including caesarean delivery, preeclampsia, preterm delivery and obstetric hemorrhage. Differences in access to care, health education, preventive resources and supportive community environments likely contribute.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Caesarean delivery is among the complications associated with socioeconomic disadvantage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lower socioeconomic status has been associated with higher, not lower, rates of preeclampsia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Preterm delivery has been associated with lower socioeconomic status, not reduced by it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Socioeconomic factors are associated with higher rates of unintended pregnancy in lower-SES groups.

questions.topicName: Social Determinants of Sexual and Reproductive Health

questions.stem: Two years after a new long-acting HIV prevention medication became available, a state reports falling HIV incidence in insured urban residents but no change among uninsured rural residents. Which of the following best explains the difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Inaccurate reporting of urban HIV incidence

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lower drug efficacy in rural populations

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lower HIV exposure among uninsured groups

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rapid viral resistance in rural communities

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unequal access, uptake and continuity of care

explanation.summary: New prevention tools expand options, but their population-level impact depends on healthcare access, patient engagement and continuity of care.
explanation.whyCorrect: Emerging prevention strategies can expand options to reduce sexual health disparities, but their effectiveness at the population level depends on healthcare access, patient engagement and continuity of care. Because biomedical innovations are used unevenly across groups with different resources, their impact can widen or leave disparities unchanged unless underlying barriers are addressed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: There is no reason to doubt the data; unequal access explains the pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The drug's biologic efficacy does not depend on residence; the gap reflects access and continuity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Uninsured status is not protective; the lecture ties such gaps to unequal access to care.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nothing suggests resistance; the pattern follows insurance and geography, pointing to access.

questions.topicName: Social Determinants of Sexual and Reproductive Health

questions.stem: A 23-year-old man who is gay, lives in a rural area, works a low-wage hourly job and belongs to a racial minority group has had difficulty obtaining sexual health care. His clinician recognizes that these identities and circumstances overlap and compound one another rather than acting separately. Which of the following concepts best describes this recognition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allostatic load

choices.label: B
choices.text: Health literacy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Implicit bias

choices.label: D
choices.text: Intersectionality

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rural isolation

explanation.summary: Intersectionality describes how multiple social identities and circumstances interact to shape barriers and outcomes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sexual and reproductive health outcomes are shaped by multiple interacting social, economic and healthcare-related factors, and differences have been documented across demographic groups, including sexual and gender minority populations. Intersectionality is the framework for recognizing that overlapping identities and circumstances, such as rurality, poverty, race and sexual orientation, combine to create barriers; rurality, for example, may interact with poverty and stigma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Allostatic load describes the physiologic toll of chronic stress, not how overlapping identities combine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Health literacy concerns understanding health information, not overlapping social positions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Implicit bias is an unconscious attitude in a clinician, not the interaction of a patient's multiple identities.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rural geography is only one of his several overlapping circumstances.

questions.topicName: Social Determinants of Sexual and Reproductive Health

questions.stem: A county with rising STI rates among 18- to 24-year-olds is choosing a program to improve young adults' sexual health. Which of the following approaches is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Abstinence-only curricula delivered through local high schools

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fee-based STI testing offered at one central county clinic

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mandatory parental consent for all STI testing in young adults

choices.label: D
choices.text: Partner notification carried out by local law enforcement

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transportation help, free STI testing and comprehensive education

explanation.summary: Programs providing transportation, free STI testing and comprehensive education to young adults could improve sexual health outcomes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Interventions that improve access to resources and preventive services, including vaccinations, contraception, reproductive healthcare and comprehensive sexual health education, are associated with better outcomes. Programs providing transportation, free STI testing and comprehensive education to young adults could improve sexual health outcomes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The lecture supports comprehensive sexual health education, not abstinence-only instruction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fees and a single distant site add cost and transportation barriers rather than removing them.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Adding consent hurdles creates a barrier; the goal is to make testing more accessible.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Involving law enforcement increases stigma and confidentiality concerns and deters care.

questions.topicName: Social Determinants of Sexual and Reproductive Health

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man tells his physician that he occasionally exchanges sex for money. He reports consistent condom use, a single regular client, and no symptoms, and he prefers to discuss screening options before deciding. A colleague suggests enrolling him in an intensive monthly STI screening protocol based on his disclosure alone. Which of the following is the most appropriate approach?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Defer screening until he stops exchanging sex so that results are reliable

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enroll him in monthly full STI panels because he exchanges sex for money

choices.label: C
choices.text: Require monthly HIV testing as a condition of ongoing care at the clinic

choices.label: D
choices.text: Screen only if he develops symptoms, since he reports consistent condom use

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tailor counseling and screening to his exposures and preferences

explanation.summary: Evidence is insufficient for prevention recommendations based solely on commercial or survival sex; use an individualized approach based on exposures and preferences.
explanation.whyCorrect: Clinicians should avoid assumptions about a person's circumstances, autonomy or risk based solely on disclosure of commercial or survival sex. Current evidence is insufficient to support prevention recommendations based only on that participation, so clinicians should individualize care using the patient's circumstances, preferences and potential exposures while ensuring access to counseling, screening and prevention services.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Deferring leaves him without screening; prevention services should be offered now.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Evidence does not support prevention recommendations based solely on participation in commercial or survival sex.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Conditions on care are coercive; care should be voluntary and patient-centered.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Waiting for symptoms ignores asymptomatic infection; an individualized plan still offers screening.

questions.topicName: Social Determinants of Sexual and Reproductive Health

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman who injects drugs and exchanges sex for shelter presents with a skin abscess at an injection site. She has no stable housing and says she is not ready to stop using drugs. Which of the following plans best reflects patient-centered, voluntary care?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Discharge with advice to return once she has housing

choices.label: B
choices.text: Referral to police to address her housing arrangement

choices.label: C
choices.text: Withholding condoms to avoid encouraging sex work

choices.label: D
choices.text: Wound care only after she agrees to stop using drugs

choices.label: E
choices.text: Wound care, substance-use services and a housing referral

explanation.summary: Patients should have voluntary, patient-centered access to services such as wound care, substance-use services, condoms and referrals for housing, food, transportation and legal or violence-prevention help.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients should have access to condoms, lubricant, vaccinations, contraception, pregnancy-related care, wound care and substance-use services, plus referrals for housing, food, transportation, legal assistance or violence prevention when appropriate. Care should be patient-centered, voluntary and responsive to individual needs, aiming to reduce harms and support informed decisions.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Deferring care leaves her infection and needs unaddressed; she should be helped now.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Involving police raises criminalization concerns and damages trust in care.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Condoms and lubricant are among the preventive services patients should be able to access.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Making care conditional on abstinence is coercive; services should be voluntary and responsive to her needs.

questions.topicName: Social Determinants of Sexual and Reproductive Health

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl comes for a sports physical. She mentions privately that she has been sexually active with one partner. Which of the following is the most appropriate approach to her sexual health?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Defer any sexual history until she reaches adulthood at 18

choices.label: B
choices.text: Discuss sexual health only after contacting her parents first

choices.label: C
choices.text: Discuss sexual health only if she reports genital symptoms

choices.label: D
choices.text: Give her the chance to discuss her sexual history and concerns

choices.label: E
choices.text: Limit the discussion to contraception and skip her history

explanation.summary: Every sexually active adult or adolescent should be given the opportunity to talk about their sexual history and concerns.
explanation.whyCorrect: Many visits involve sexual issues, and every sexually active adult or adolescent should be given the opportunity to talk about their sexual history and any concerns. Although the topic can be uncomfortable, it is crucial to a complete workup and supports patient-centered care.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Every sexually active adolescent should have the opportunity to discuss sexual history and concerns now.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Requiring parental involvement before discussion creates a barrier to her care.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sexual health discussion should not wait for symptoms; it is part of a complete workup.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Her sexual history and concerns are central to her workup, not only contraception.

questions.topicName: Social Determinants of Sexual and Reproductive Health

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman is prescribed HIV PrEP, and her plan lists the drug as covered. Two months later she still has not started it. She explains that the plan requires prior authorization and repeated lab tests, each lab visit means losing an hourly shift and arranging childcare, and the first two pharmacies she called did not stock it. Which of the following best characterizes her situation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A clinical contraindication that makes PrEP inappropriate for her at this time

choices.label: B
choices.text: A knowledge deficit that education about PrEP efficacy would reliably resolve

choices.label: C
choices.text: A personal choice to decline PrEP that should be documented as an informed refusal

choices.label: D
choices.text: An insurance denial that leaves her without coverage for the prescribed drug

choices.label: E
choices.text: An on-formulary drug that remains unusable because obtaining it has hidden costs

explanation.summary: Income affects health beyond paying a bill: a covered medication may still be unusable because of lost shifts, childcare, labs, authorization and pharmacy stocking.
explanation.whyCorrect: A patient may have access to a medication in theory but still be unable to use it because obtaining care requires missing an hourly shift, paying for transportation, arranging childcare, traveling, paying deductibles or copayments, repeated laboratory testing, navigating insurance authorization and finding a pharmacy that stocks the drug. Eligibility and coverage do not automatically translate into access.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Nothing in the stem suggests a clinical contraindication; the obstacles are practical and economic.
whyWrongByChoice.B: She understands and wants PrEP; education does not remove lost wages, childcare or authorization steps.
whyWrongByChoice.C: She has not declined PrEP; barriers are preventing her from obtaining it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The drug is covered; her barriers arise from what is required to actually obtain and use it.

questions.topicName: Social Determinants of Sexual and Reproductive Health

questions.stem: A physician is taking a sexual history from a 24-year-old woman whose partners are unknown to the physician. Which of the following opening questions best reflects respectful, neutral language that avoids assumptions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: I assume you only have sex with men, right?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Is your boyfriend your only sexual partner right now?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tell me about your current sexual partners, if any.

choices.label: D
choices.text: You and your husband are monogamous, correct?

choices.label: E
choices.text: You don't have any risky partners, do you?

explanation.summary: Interpersonal stigma reduction uses respectful, neutral language that avoids assumptions about partners.
explanation.whyCorrect: At the interpersonal level, health professionals address stigma by using respectful, neutral language and avoiding assumptions. An open question about current partners allows the patient to describe her relationships accurately, whereas questions that presume partner gender, marital status or monogamy can deter disclosure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This explicitly assumes her partners' gender and can alienate patients.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This assumes she has a male partner, which may discourage accurate disclosure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This assumes both marital status and monogamy rather than asking openly.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This leading, judgmental phrasing invites a false reassurance rather than an honest history.

questions.topicName: Social Determinants of Sexual and Reproductive Health

questions.stem: A health equity researcher studies adults who have lived for decades with poverty, food insecurity and racial discrimination. According to the allostatic load model, which of the following findings is most expected in this group compared with similar adults without these exposures?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increased inflammation along with epigenetic changes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lower cortisol exposure along with stable metabolism

choices.label: C
choices.text: Protective epigenetic changes along with lower disease risk

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reduced inflammation along with enhanced immune function

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stable endocrine function along with lower cardiac risk

explanation.summary: Allostatic load is associated with endocrine, cardiovascular, immune and metabolic dysregulation, increased inflammation and epigenetic changes that raise chronic disease risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: Adverse social determinants such as poverty, housing instability, food insecurity, discrimination and chronic stress persistently activate the HPA axis and prolong cortisol exposure. The resulting allostatic load is associated with endocrine, cardiovascular, immune and metabolic dysregulation, increased inflammation and epigenetic changes that may increase the risk of chronic disease and adverse outcomes.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Chronic stress causes prolonged cortisol exposure and metabolic dysregulation, not stability.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The epigenetic changes linked to allostatic load may increase, not decrease, chronic disease risk.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Allostatic load is associated with increased inflammation and immune dysregulation, not enhanced immunity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Allostatic load is associated with endocrine and cardiovascular dysregulation.

questions.topicName: Social Determinants of Sexual and Reproductive Health

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with a wrist sprain. She discloses that the man she dated until last year still follows her to work, tracks her phone, and recently shoved her into a wall. Which form of gender-based violence does her experience represent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Community violence

choices.label: B
choices.text: Harmful cultural practice

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intimate partner violence

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sex trafficking

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sexual exploitation

explanation.summary: Intimate partner violence, the most common form of GBV, includes stalking, coercive control, and physical violence by a current or former partner.
explanation.whyCorrect: Intimate partner violence encompasses physical violence, sexual violence, stalking, coercive control, or psychological harm by a current OR former intimate partner. Following her, tracking her phone, and shoving her are stalking, controlling behavior, and physical violence by an ex-partner. IPV is the most common form of gender-based violence.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The perpetrator is a former intimate partner, which defines IPV rather than violence from the community.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Harmful cultural practices are practices such as FGM, forced marriage, or virginity testing, not an ex-partner's stalking.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sex trafficking involves commercial or other sexual activity obtained by force, fraud, or coercion; no sexual activity is described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sexual exploitation involves sexual activity where meaningful consent cannot be given; none is described.

questions.topicName: Gender-Based Violence, Trauma Informed Care, & Ethical Principles of Medical Care

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man tells his primary care physician during an annual visit that he was sexually assaulted at a party 3 weeks ago. He becomes tearful and stops talking. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acknowledge his experience and offer support

choices.label: B
choices.text: Arrange forensic evidence collection at once

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ask him to describe the assault in full detail

choices.label: D
choices.text: Begin a genital examination to look for injury

choices.label: E
choices.text: Contact law enforcement to file a police report

explanation.summary: The first step in caring for any person who has experienced violence is to acknowledge their experience and create a supportive environment.
explanation.whyCorrect: The lecture states the first step in caring for a patient who has experienced violence is to acknowledge their experience and create a supportive, respectful environment. Gender-based violence can affect people of any gender, so a male survivor is approached the same way.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Forensic collection is offered when indicated and desired by the patient, not imposed as the first step.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Patients should share information at their own pace; demanding a full detailed account first is not trauma-informed.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Examination requires consent and comes after the patient feels safe; it is not the first step.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Medical care is not contingent on law enforcement involvement, and reporting an adult's assault is not the initial response.

questions.topicName: Gender-Based Violence, Trauma Informed Care, & Ethical Principles of Medical Care

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman is transferred to the emergency department from an urgent care clinic after a sexual assault. The transfer note contains a detailed, well-documented account of the event. The emergency physician is about to take a history. Which of the following approaches is most consistent with recommended practice?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Begin by asking whether her husband was the assailant

choices.label: B
choices.text: Have her retell the full event to check its consistency

choices.label: C
choices.text: Review the note and ask open-ended questions at her pace

choices.label: D
choices.text: Start with detailed questions about her sexual history

choices.label: E
choices.text: Use a rapid series of closed yes/no questions to save time

explanation.summary: Survivors should not be made to recount adequately documented events; use open-ended, nonjudgmental questions at the patient's pace.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients should not be asked to repeatedly recount events when the relevant information has already been adequately documented. Recommended practice is to use open-ended, nonjudgmental questions and let the patient share at her own pace, avoiding unnecessary repetition.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Clinicians should avoid assumptions about relationships, gender, or the circumstances of the assault.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Repeated recounting of already documented events is specifically discouraged and risks re-traumatization.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sensitive questions should have their purpose explained and consent obtained, not lead the history.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Open-ended questions, not rapid yes/no questioning, are recommended.

questions.topicName: Gender-Based Violence, Trauma Informed Care, & Ethical Principles of Medical Care

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman is undergoing a pelvic examination after reporting a sexual assault. Midway through, she grips the table, becomes tense, and says, "I don't know if I can do this." Which of the following is the most appropriate action by the examining physician?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ask the chaperone to help hold her still in position

choices.label: B
choices.text: Explain that stopping now will lose key evidence

choices.label: C
choices.text: Finish quickly to shorten her overall period of distress

choices.label: D
choices.text: Give an anxiolytic and then complete the exam

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pause and remind her she may stop or decline any part

explanation.summary: Survivors remain in control of the examination and can pause, stop, or decline any portion of care.
explanation.whyCorrect: If a survivor is not comfortable with a procedure, the clinician should assure her she is in control and can ask to pause, stop, and decline any portion of the care. Consent is obtained before and throughout the examination, especially at sensitive portions, restoring the survivor's sense of control.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Physical restraint violates consent; a chaperone is present per policy, not to hold a patient.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pressuring her with evidence concerns is coercive; care and evidence collection are her choice.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Continuing despite distress disregards her ongoing consent and risks re-traumatization.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Medicating to push through the exam overrides her ability to pause or decline.

questions.topicName: Gender-Based Violence, Trauma Informed Care, & Ethical Principles of Medical Care

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman presents 8 hours after a sexual assault by an acquaintance. She has a scalp laceration and requests pregnancy prevention and STI testing. After discussion, she declines forensic evidence collection and does not want police involvement. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Collect evidence anyway because it is time sensitive

choices.label: B
choices.text: Discharge her with a referral to an outside SANE program

choices.label: C
choices.text: Notify police before beginning any medical treatment

choices.label: D
choices.text: Treat her injury and provide emergency contraception

choices.label: E
choices.text: Withhold treatment until she agrees to evidence collection

explanation.summary: Medical care must not be contingent on whether a patient participates in forensic evidence collection or law enforcement processes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Forensic evidence collection is performed when indicated AND desired by the patient. Medical care should not be contingent on whether the patient chooses to participate in forensic collection or law enforcement processes, so her laceration, pregnancy prevention, and STI evaluation should proceed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Evidence collection proceeds only when desired by the patient; doing it anyway violates her autonomy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: She requested care here; discharging without treating her needs abandons her.
whyWrongByChoice.C: She has declined police involvement, and treatment is not conditional on it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Making care contingent on evidence collection is explicitly contrary to the lecture.

questions.topicName: Gender-Based Violence, Trauma Informed Care, & Ethical Principles of Medical Care

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman at 30 weeks' gestation presents to the emergency department after her partner pushed her against a table during an argument. She has a small bruise on her lower abdomen, says she feels fine, and asks to go home. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Documentation of the bruise and discharge home

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ice to the bruise with bleeding-return precautions

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prompt evaluation of both the mother and the fetus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reassurance and an outpatient visit in one week

choices.label: E
choices.text: Safety planning alone without further examination

explanation.summary: Physical trauma in pregnancy, including IPV, requires prompt maternal and fetal evaluation even when injuries appear minor.
explanation.whyCorrect: GBV including IPV can cause trauma during pregnancy and increases the risk of placental abruption, preterm labor, fetal distress, low birth weight, and fetal loss. Because even seemingly minor injuries can have significant obstetric consequences, prompt maternal and fetal evaluation is required.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Documentation is appropriate but cannot replace maternal and fetal assessment.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Symptomatic care with return precautions underestimates the obstetric risk of seemingly minor trauma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Delaying evaluation a week risks missing abruption or fetal distress.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Safety planning is important but does not substitute for obstetric evaluation after trauma.

questions.topicName: Gender-Based Violence, Trauma Informed Care, & Ethical Principles of Medical Care

questions.stem: A 15-year-old girl seen at a clinic in Arkansas for pelvic pain discloses that her mother's 30-year-old boyfriend has been having sex with her for several months. She begs the physician not to tell anyone. Which of the following is the physician required to do?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Document it and reassess at her next routine visit

choices.label: B
choices.text: Keep the disclosure confidential as she requested

choices.label: C
choices.text: Refer her to her school counselor for follow-up

choices.label: D
choices.text: Report to the state child abuse hotline

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tell her mother and allow the family to decide

explanation.summary: Physicians are mandated reporters in Arkansas and must notify the Child Abuse Hotline of suspected maltreatment of anyone younger than 18.
explanation.whyCorrect: Under Arkansas law physicians are mandated reporters and must notify the Arkansas Child Abuse Hotline for suspected maltreatment of a child (birth to younger than 18), which includes sexual abuse. An adult in a caretaker/authority position having sex with a 15-year-old requires a report; confidentiality is balanced against mandatory-reporting laws that protect vulnerable individuals.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Prompt reporting is critical for the child's safety; waiting delays protection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Confidentiality must be balanced against mandatory reporting; suspected child sexual abuse must be reported.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A counselor referral does not fulfill the physician's own mandated-reporting obligation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Leaving the decision to the family does not satisfy the legal duty and may leave her unsafe.

questions.topicName: Gender-Based Violence, Trauma Informed Care, & Ethical Principles of Medical Care

questions.stem: A 17-year-old girl in Arkansas asks her physician for contraception. She has been sexually active with her 17-year-old boyfriend for 6 months. She describes the relationship as voluntary, denies pressure, threats, or gifts in exchange for sex, and feels safe at home and school. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decline contraception until she reaches age of majority

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inform her parents because she is legally a minor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Perform a genital exam to screen for signs of abuse

choices.label: D
choices.text: Provide contraceptive care; no automatic report is implied

choices.label: E
choices.text: Report to the hotline because she is younger than 18 years

explanation.summary: Minor status does not bar participation in sexual health care, and sexual activity in a minor is not automatic proof of abuse.
explanation.whyCorrect: Key takeaways: minor status does not equal inability to participate in sexual health care, and sexual activity in a minor does not equal automatic proof of abuse. The clinician assesses age, age difference, voluntariness, coercion, capacity, power differential, exploitation, and immediate safety; here none suggests abuse, so she should receive the care she requested.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Minor status does not preclude participation in sexual health care or decisions.
